cards.front: What type must an if condition be in Java?
cards.extra: There is no truthiness: if (1) is a compile error, unlike C. A non-boolean needs an explicit comparison.
cards.example:
boolean ready = true;
if (ready) { System.out.println("go"); }
// if (1) { } // error: an if condition must be boolean

cards.front: In an if / else-if chain, how many branches run?
cards.back: Exactly one — the first whose condition is true, then the rest are skipped
cards.extra: That is why order matters: a broad condition placed first shadows every later one.
cards.example:
int n = 2;
if (n == 1) { System.out.println("first"); }
else if (n == 2) { System.out.println("second"); }
else { System.out.println("other"); } // skipped: one branch only

cards.front: What are Java's three loop statements?
cards.extra: All three repeat a body; they differ in where the condition sits and what they make easy to express.
cards.example:
int n = 3;
for (int i = 0; i != n; i++) { }
while (n != 0) { n--; }
do { n++; } while (n != 1);

cards.front: What are the three parts of a for loop header?
cards.back: Initialisation; condition; update — for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
cards.extra: All three are optional. Omit the condition entirely and you get an infinite loop.
cards.example:
int n = 3;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { // init; condition; update
  System.out.println(i);
}

cards.front: When does a while loop's body never run?
cards.back: When the condition is false on the first check
cards.extra: The condition is tested before each pass, so zero iterations is a normal outcome.
cards.example:
int n = 0;
while (n > 0) {
  n--; // never runs: condition false on the first check
}

cards.back: The body runs at least once, because the condition is checked afterwards
cards.extra: Use it when the first pass must happen — a menu that has to be displayed before the user can choose Exit.
cards.example:
int i = 0;
do { i++; } while (i == 0);
System.out.println(i); // 1 - body ran before the condition was checked

cards.back: for when the number of iterations is known; while when it depends on a condition
cards.extra: Both can do the same job, but the one that states the intent costs the reader less.
cards.example:
for (int i = 0; i != 10; i++) { System.out.println(i); } // known count
int n = 10;
while (n > 0) { n--; } // depends on a condition

cards.front: What does continue do inside a loop?
cards.back: Skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the update/condition step
cards.extra: The loop keeps running — unlike break, which ends it. Beware: in a while loop, forgetting the update before continue gives an infinite loop.
cards.example:
for (int i = 0; i != 3; i++) {
  if (i == 1) { continue; } // skip print, jump to i++
  System.out.println(i);
}

cards.front: How does the menu-loop pattern in the calculator program work?
cards.back: while (true) around a menu plus a break for the Exit option
cards.extra: The loop is infinite by design; the exit branch is the only way out.

cards.front: When does a switch's default branch run?
cards.extra: It is optional, and its position is arbitrary — but placing it last is the convention readers expect.
cards.example:
int n = 3;
switch (n) {
 case 1: System.out.println("one"); break;
 default: System.out.println("other"); // no case matched
}

cards.front: Can a switch be nested inside a case?
cards.back: Yes — a switch may appear inside a case body, and break then exits only the inner switch
cards.extra: The unlabelled break binds to the nearest enclosing switch or loop, which is a common source of fall-through bugs.
cards.example:
int a = 1, b = 2;
switch (a) {
 case 1:
  switch (b) { case 2: System.out.println("inner"); break; }
  System.out.println("after inner switch"); break; // inner break only
}
